articles.title: Europe views US with ‘much less horror’ after Trump’s midterms defeat
articles.summary: But experts say Washington’s shift away from Europe runs deeper than Trump and is unlikely to be reversed.
articles.body:
During the campaign for the midterm elections in the United States, neither the Democrats nor the Republicans spoke much about issues related to Europe.

US President Donald Trump’s handling of the Ukraine war, his approach to Greenland and his aggressive posture towards the European Union were not on the agenda.

Yet while the Democratic Party’s victory last week could produce a Congress that is friendlier towards Europe, experts do not expect major shifts in US foreign policy in some areas.

“Europeans are looking much less in horror towards the US than they have in the past two years, but they should not exaggerate the significance in terms of transatlantic relations,” said Erik Jones, director of the Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies at the European University Institute. “The trend line has been moving in a consistent direction across administrations, and this midterm election does not change that trend.”

For decades, the transatlantic relationship was built on the assumption that Washington needed a free, prosperous and secure Europe, while European governments relied on American security guarantees.

But that consensus has gradually eroded, and it did not start with Trump. Over time, there was a loss of popular support for global engagement on both sides of the Atlantic.

The pattern began under Barack Obama, whose administration started a strategic reorientation towards Asia, analysts say, because of perceived threats to US security from the region. That has become a rare area of agreement across the political divide: Republicans and Democrats alike support Europeans taking greater responsibility for their own security.

The US president has accelerated that shift with his America First approach. He has repeatedly lashed out at NATO, threatened to seize Greenland and has shown greater respect for Russia than Ukraine, undermining European efforts to isolate and weaken Moscow.

A Democratic-controlled Congress will have more power over federal spending, legislation and congressional oversight to challenge some of Trump’s decisions. But the president would retain considerable authority over foreign policy.

“All speak in favour of better transatlantic ties, more predictable and more open to take into account European expectations from America,” said Fredrik Erixon, an economist and director of the European Centre for International Political Economy, noting that the Democrats lack a veto-proof majority. “But on issues such as Ukraine, Iran and tariffs there is still a lot of space for the president to behave in the same fashion as in past years.”

With the Iran war, which has pushed up global energy prices, there is no easy way out.

Trump could either cut a deal and declare victory, potentially leaving Iran with leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, or resume military action – a deeply unpopular prospect among US voters. In either scenario, European allies are left with a cost of living crisis that is driving protests across the continent.

Some Democrats have discussed using the next government funding bill to block flows for the war in Iran, a proposal that is popular with antiwar lawmakers.

In Ukraine, the new Democrat-dominated Congress may favour greater support for Kyiv, but that support may not be a game changer for the war-torn nation. Ukrainian officials are anxious about the two-month window before the new Congress takes office in January and fear that Trump could use the period to pursue further talks with Putin.

Even so, the Democrats are likely to invest more energy in improving social services and economic conditions at home.

Some experts also suggest that a politically weakened Trump may now look abroad to demonstrate strength, score wins and build his legacy. His domestic electoral setback could therefore translate into an even less predictable and less accommodating foreign policy.

Last week, the US president said there would soon be a “big, beautiful agreement” on Ukraine, one that “might involve all of Europe”. The comments came ahead of trilateral talks between Ukrainian, Russian and US officials in Abu Dhabi, which have so far failed to yield any breakthrough.

The prospect of a broader deal has raised questions about how much say European governments would have in negotiations that affect their security.

“Trump’s moves are difficult to predict,” said Michele Valensise, president of the Institute for International Affairs and former secretary-general of Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. “It is important for Europeans to be involved in the ongoing contacts aimed at ending the war launched by Russia against Ukraine.”

“We shall see whether the American administration will now accommodate this strong European expectation or choose to ignore it, opting to negotiate exclusively with Russia – a scenario that would unfairly weaken the position of the European allies.”

That uncertainty extends beyond Ukraine.

The Pentagon is expected to complete its review of US military forces in Europe next month, potentially paving the way for decisions on the size and distribution of its footprint.

On tariffs, too, the political divide has shifted.

Democrats have traditionally been more protective of US manufacturing and workers, while Republicans were historically more closely associated with free trade. Trump’s first administration blurred that distinction, and Democrats have since moved towards a more protectionist position on trade.

But even if US courts strike down some of Trump’s tariffs, Europe may see little immediate relief. The trade agreement negotiated between Washington and Brussels is a different matter, Erixon said, because it involves the commitments made by both sides rather than tariffs imposed unilaterally by the US.

“That needs to be renegotiated for tariffs to be taken off, and the US administration will not initiate such a process in the next two years,” he said.

For Jones, the question is not whether the Democrats’ victory will improve relations with Europe, but what Europeans will do with the time it has given them.

“This is better, but how much better? And what should Europe do with the time that this election has bought them?” he said. “Should they use it to repair transatlantic relations? That would be time wasted. They should use this time to prepare for when the US will care even less.”

articles.title: Alejandro Blanco: "Lo más importante de los comités olímpicos es su identidad"
articles.standfirst: El presidente español ambiciona presidir la Asamblea de Comités Olímpicos Nacionales en las elecciones del 8 de diciembre
articles.summary: El presidente español ambiciona presidir la Asamblea de Comités Olímpicos Nacionales en las elecciones del 8 de diciembre
articles.body: alejandro Blanco (Ourense, 1950), presidente del Comité Olímpico Español, se ha presentado a 24 elecciones y las ha ganado todas. La vigésimoquinta, el 8 de diciembre en Hong Kong, es la más pomposa de todas. Pretende presidir la asamblea de todos los comités olímpicos nacionales del mundo, 206 en total. Como rival tendrá al argelino Mustapha Berraf. Pregunta: ¿Qué le ha llevado a dar el paso para presentarse a la presidencia de ANOC? Respuesta: No estaba entre mis pensamientos presentar esta candidatura. Sin embargo, ha habido un movimiento muy fuerte en Europa y América que me ha propuesto como candidato. Después tuve una reunión con la presidenta (Coventry) para hablar de las posibilidades de ANOC. También muchas personas de distintos continentes hablaron conmigo porque me veían como el mejor candidato. Finalmente, he dado el paso adelante. Me ha sorprendido la fuerza de la propuesta de Europa, América y otros comités olímpicos. Pero ya hemos tomado la decisión y vamos a intentar ganar el próximo 8 de diciembre. P. Precisamente, resulta sorprendente que hasta ahora no haya habido ningún presidente europeo al frente de ANOC. R. ANOC ha tenido dos presidentes. El primero fue mi querido Mario Vázquez Raña, que estuvo más de 30 años. Luego Ahmad Al-Fahad Al-Sabah, y después llegó el tercer presidente, Robin Mitchell, que ha sido una especie de paso intermedio. Nunca ha habido un presidente europeo. Vamos a ver si ahora rompemos ese techo y conseguimos que el nuevo presidente sea europeo y, sobre todo, español. P.: Nos sorprendió a todos el acuerdo y luego el desacuerdo que se planteó con Mustapha. ¿A qué se debió? R.: Creo que el acuerdo era un buen planteamiento. Mi amigo Mustapha contaba con el apoyo de África y Asia, mientras que a mí me apoyaban Europa y América. No se veía tanto como una lucha entre dos candidatos, sino como un enfrentamiento entre dos continentes y otros dos. Y creo que eso no era bueno para el movimiento olímpico. Era mejor alcanzar un acuerdo, hacer una transición tranquila y preparar el futuro. ¿Qué ocurrió? Que, cuando planteamos el acuerdo, Europa y América dijeron que no querían llegar a él y que preferían celebrar elecciones. Muchos presidentes de comités olímpicos de África y Asia dijeron lo mismo. El acuerdo estaba pensado única y exclusivamente para evitar ese enfrentamiento y hacer una transición tranquila. Si la gente quería elecciones, sabíamos que tendríamos que ir a ellas. P.: Sonaba a que había un enfrentamiento entre los dos. R. No, para nada. Nosotros llegamos a un acuerdo. Tengo muy buena relación con Mustapha y habíamos hablado de ello para evitar unas elecciones duras, en un momento en el que lo más conveniente era hacer una transición tranquila y preparar el futuro. Había que escuchar a los comités olímpicos. Esa era la decisión y no pasa nada. Hay algo que alguna vez he visto publicado: el acuerdo solo era posible si se cumplían los estatutos y los principios de buen gobierno. Es decir, no se iba a hacer nada en contra de las normas. Existía la posibilidad de alcanzar un acuerdo conforme a la legislación suiza. Pero si la gente quiere elecciones, por mí, encantado. P. En su candidatura habla de credibilidad, consenso, compromiso, cercanía y cambio.¿Qué mejoras cree que se pueden introducir? R. Más allá de las mejoras puntuales que se pueden hacer, creo que el anterior ejecutivo de ANOC, del que formaba parte, ha realizado un trabajo extraordinario y ha elaborado un plan estratégico magnífico de cara al futuro, que además asumo totalmente. Pero creo que el problema de ANOC no es una cuestión concreta: es un problema de identidad. Al final, tenemos que poner en valor la importancia que tienen los comités olímpicos. Sabemos que existen tres grandes pilares: el Comité Olímpico Internacional (CIO), que es el paraguas; los deportistas; las federaciones internacionales y los comités olímpicos. Además, hay un cuarto pilar que no podemos olvidar: los gobiernos. Si analizas el programa de la presidenta Coventry y todo lo que quiere hacer durante estos ocho años, no podrá llevarlo a cabo sin los comités olímpicos. El paso del deporte a la sociedad se realiza a través de ellos. El vehículo que conecta el deporte con la sociedad y, a la inversa, la sociedad con el CIO son los comités olímpicos. Lo más importante es darles identidad: saber quiénes somos, qué representamos, cómo podemos hacerlo mejor y cómo podemos establecer las líneas de relación con los gobiernos. Vivimos una situación mundial muy complicada e inestable. El deporte está en medio de esa realidad y tiene que ser garante de la construcción de una sociedad mejor, a través de sus valores. Los auténticos embajadores de esta tarea son los comités olímpicos. Por eso, más allá de los 20 puntos que llevamos en el programa, creo que ANOC tiene que recuperar su identidad, su importancia y su peso específico dentro del CIO. P. Precisamente, da la sensación de que, dentro de esos tres pilares sobre los que se construye el movimiento olímpico, los comités olímpicos quizá han sido los más débiles. R. Creo que tienen que ser los más fuertes. Los deportistas siempre están en primer lugar, pero los comités olímpicos tienen que estar a su altura. No podemos pensar que se puede hacer lo que se quiera y trasladarlo a la sociedad sin contar con los comités olímpicos. Y sé que ni la presidenta ni los anteriores presidentes piensan así. Esa es precisamente la identidad que quiero recalcar. Después están los 20 puntos que mencionas, las cinco ces, cada una de las cuales incluye entre cuatro y cinco objetivos. Pero lo más importante para mí es dotar a ANOC de identidad. Por ejemplo, una cuestión fundamental es que el presidente de ANOC no pueda ser miembro del CIO. ¿Por qué? Porque, aunque tenemos que estar al cien por cien con el CIO, también debemos preservar nuestra independencia. Y esa independencia se garantiza, entre otras cosas, cuando el presidente no es miembro de esa asamblea. Debe ser un presidente de un comité olímpico. P. ¿Por qué debe ser un presidente de un comité olímpico? R. Porque así habla en nombre de los comités olímpicos. Si no es presidente de un comité olímpico, habla sobre ellos, pero no vive su día a día. No puedes ser presidente de ANOC si no tienes un despacho en el que cada día recibes a un deportista, gestionas asuntos con empresas y trabajas con los gobiernos y los patrocinadores. Si no vives ese día a día, es muy difícil trasladarlo. Por eso, una de las grandes propuestas es que el presidente de ANOC sea presidente de un comité olímpico y no sea miembro del CIO. De esta manera garantizamos algo muy importante para mí: la independencia. Eso no significa que no tengamos que estar con el CIO. Al contrario, nuestro compromiso debe ser absoluto. Pero la voz que vamos a llevar será la de los comités olímpicos. Por ejemplo, el CIO tiene una serie de comisiones y ha llevado a cabo una reducción de las mismas. Yo propongo que en cada comisión haya dos representantes de los comités olímpicos. Pero esos representantes no deben ser elegidos por el CIO, sino por ANOC. Es decir, las personas que representen a los comités olímpicos en las comisiones del CIO tienen que ser elegidas por los propios comités olímpicos. Se trata de darles identidad y carácter propio. Somos los comités olímpicos. Esto es lo que pensamos y lo que queremos trasladar, siempre desde la máxima lealtad y con la máxima confianza en la presidenta para que pueda desarrollar todo su trabajo. P: ¿Se puede asegurar la independencia en todos los países y también con el CIO, dado que es el único motor económico de muchos comités? R. Creo que la perfección no existe, pero se puede intentar. Lo que tenemos que conseguir es que los comités olímpicos, a través del CIO y del programa TOP, dispongan de recursos que les permitan ser fuertes. Porque, si no eres fuerte y eres débil, eres dependiente. Eso es lo más importante. En segundo lugar, hay algo que considero fundamental y que creo que esta casa ha hecho muy bien, algo que también se ha reconocido internacionalmente: tenemos que definir cuáles son las líneas de trabajo con los gobiernos. Cuando hablo de independencia no me refiero a que el movimiento deportivo tenga que estar alejado de los gobiernos. En absoluto. No podremos llevar el deporte a toda la sociedad sin contar con ellos. Es imposible. Por eso, cuando se habla de tres pilares, yo siempre incorporo un cuarto: los gobiernos. Sin ellos no se podría hacer nada. Pero hay que definir claramente cuál es la línea de colaboración con los gobiernos y dónde termina esa colaboración y comienza la injerencia. Creo que es algo muy importante. Cuando existe un conflicto entre un comité olímpico y un gobierno, y sabes que he intervenido en muchos de estos conflictos, considero que no debe actuar únicamente una persona del Comité Olímpico Internacional. Tiene que existir una comisión en la que estén representados el CIO y ANOC, así como el comité olímpico continental, para definir una línea de actuación. La colaboración tiene que ser máxima. La injerencia se produce cuando un gobierno quiere intervenir, dominar o hacer lo que quiera dentro del movimiento deportivo. P. ¿Hay que adaptar el modelo a cada país? R.: Hay que adaptarlo, porque cada país es diferente. Pero, para que un comité olímpico sea independiente, lo primero que necesita son medios para mantener una estructura y poder actuar con independencia. Si no dispone de ellos, evidentemente, queda sometido o debilitado. P. ¿Qué aprendió, sobre todo, de Mario Vázquez Raña como presidente de ANOC? R.: Mario era un hombre muy poderoso y pertenecía a otra época. El movimiento deportivo también era diferente. Era un hombre con una gran autoridad, con un enorme amor por el movimiento olímpico y que realizó una labor extraordinaria. Si tuviera que quedarme con algo de Mario, aunque me quedaría con muchas cosas, sería con el amor que tenía por el olimpismo y con la manera en que defendía a los comités olímpicos. P. Cuando vino la presidenta Coventry a Madrid, ¿de qué hablaron? R. Hablamos de lo que pienso sobre ANOC. De su identidad.Y algo tan importante como esa identidad es que no puede vivir sin el CIO. El vehículo que tiene el CIO para desarrollar toda su política son los comités olímpicos nacionales. Por eso tenemos que estar unidos, perfectamente alineados. Quien marca las directrices del movimiento olímpico es el CIO, en este caso su presidenta, y nosotros tenemos que seguir esas líneas. P. ¿Le salen las cuentas? R. Las cuentas me saldrán el día que se abra la urna y salgan las papeletas. Creo que estamos disputando el partido, utilizando una expresión deportiva, y que tenemos posibilidades de ganar. Dicho esto, Mustafa es un buen candidato y seguro que también tiene muchos apoyos. No será una victoria fácil para ninguno de los dos. P. ¿Dejará la presidencia del Comité Olímpico Español si gana? R. La base es que tienes que seguir siendo presidente de un comité olímpico. Creo que, si tuviera que elegir —aunque no tengo que hacerlo porque ya lo he hablado—, para mí lo más importante es esta casa. Si tengo la suerte de ganar, tendré otra misión, pero no podría entender ANOC sin poder trasladar toda la experiencia del Comité Olímpico Español. Eso me obligará, sin ninguna duda, a trabajar más y a viajar más. Pero el COE es sagrado. P. Por esa máxima, si el 8 de diciembre, si resulta vencedor, ¿se podrá decir también que Alejandro Blanco se volverá a presentar para presidir el Comité Olímpico Español? R. No. Alejandro Blanco tiene mandato aqui hasta mayo de 2029. Lo que se podrá decir es que Alejandro Blanco, si Dios le da salud, estará hasta mayo de 2029. Después ya veremos.

articles.title: Dem rep blames 'horrific' traffic for missing Hegseth impeachment vote: 'I am so sorry'
articles.summary: Rep. Melanie Stansbury apologized in a video for missing the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, blaming rush-hour traffic and a police motorcade near the Capitol.
articles.body: Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., apologized in a social media video Wednesday for missing a key House vote on an effort to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying she encountered heavy traffic and a police motorcade while trying to reach the Capitol. "Let me start by saying, I am so sorry," Stansbury said in the video posted Wednesday. "There is no one who is more disappointed in myself than me, that I was not here the moment that gavel dropped." The House voted 211-204 Tuesday to refer the impeachment resolution introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to the Judiciary Committee, effectively blocking the effort. Stansbury was among 11 Democrats who missed the vote, along with seven Republicans. HOUSE GOP LEADERS BLOCK MASSIE'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH Stansbury said she was driving toward the Capitol ahead of the vote when she encountered "horrific" rush-hour traffic on Independence Avenue, where a lane closure had contributed to congestion. "As the vote was approaching, I ran back to my car," Stansbury said. "I got in my car, and I began driving towards the Capitol and as I approached the Capitol, it was rush hour on Independence Avenue. They closed one of the lanes. I was stuck in the right-hand lane." The congresswoman said she could see the Capitol from her vehicle and instructed her staff to notify House officials that she was delayed. A police motorcade escorting a bus away from the Capitol complex then blocked traffic in both directions, she said. "I should have been there sooner," Stansbury acknowledged. "I understand that it is my responsibility, and I am sincerely sorry, but there were definitely factors that were out of my control." DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY Several Democrats who missed the vote were returning from an Elect Democratic Women event about 1.5 miles from the Capitol when they encountered bumper-to-bumper traffic on Independence Avenue, Axios reporter Andrew Solender reported, citing multiple lawmakers. Some lawmakers found alternative ways to reach the Capitol after traffic brought their vehicles to a standstill, according to Solender. One got out and walked, while another was dropped off on the Senate side of the Capitol to avoid the congestion. The 11 Democrats who missed the vote were Stansbury and Reps. Marilyn Strickland of Washington, Julia Brownley and Lou Correa of California, Laura Gillen of New York, Steven Horsford of Nevada, Jonathan Jackson of Illinois, Nancy Pelosi of California, Brittany Pettersen of Colorado, Haley Stevens of Michigan and Frederica Wilson of Florida. Stansbury also acknowledged that Democrats lacked the votes to advance the impeachment effort even if she had been present. "We did not have the numbers to move forward to impeach Pete Hegseth at this moment," she said, also noting that a conviction in the Senate would require a two-thirds majority. HEGSETH THWARTS GOP-LED IMPEACHMENT PUSH AS QUESTIONS SWIRL OVER WHETHER ALLEGATIONS RISE TO HIGH CRIMES Massie's resolution included eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of misconduct related to U.S. military operations, including the war in Iran and strikes in Yemen and Venezuela. Hegseth rejected the allegations during a Pentagon news conference Tuesday, characterizing the impeachment effort as an attack on the military. "This is not patriotism," Hegseth said. "This is sabotage." President Donald Trump also defended Hegseth and celebrated the House vote, describing the outcome on social media as an exoneration of the defense secretary. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The vote comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate in January, potentially setting the stage for another impeachment attempt.

articles.title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moves to a military base amid Iranian threats
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base following threats from Iran, according to a source familiar with the situation.
articles.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base following threats from Iran, according to a source familiar with the situation. The move, first reported by The New York Times, marks the latest instance of a Cabinet official reportedly moving to military housing. The Atlantic previously reported that now-chief of staff Stephen Miller and former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem lived in military housing. The New York Times has also reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth live in military housing. The source familiar with Bessent’s move told NBC News that the concerns arose after The Wall Street Journal published a story that included a photo that allowed the secretary’s D.C. home to be geolocated. After the photo’s publication, the source said that “security concerns began to increase which have now forced the Secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety.” “The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials,” the source added. Dow Jones, the parent company of The Wall Street Journal, declined to comment. A spokesperson for the Treasury Department said that Bessent “will not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran’s economy.” The department has not revealed the nature of the threats that led to the move. Iranian threats have also led to the U.S. relocating military aircrafts. Just days ago, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC that several military aircraft were moved from a U.S. base in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran. Last month, two men were charged with allegedly trying to help Iran in the United Kingdom after a security incident near the same U.S. base. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the time that there were strong indications that Iran played a role in the incident. This summer, President Donald Trump took a secret flight out of Turkey amid security concerns over the war with Iran. Asked if he knew of credible threats against him from Iran, Trump said there was “a threat all the time” and that he is “No. 1 on their list.”

articles.title: Putin suggests no Ukraine compromise in meeting with US envoys
articles.summary: Vladimir Putin indicated Thursday that Russia will not compromise on its hardline demands to end the Ukraine offensive, but offered a short-term ceasefire in...
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin indicated Thursday that Russia will not compromise on its hardline demands to end the Ukraine offensive, but offered a short-term ceasefire in a key frontline city during a Kremlin meeting with US envoys.

The Russian president said he would not water down his territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine that Russia claims to have annexed, and ruled out agreeing to foreign peacekeeping troops being stationed in Ukraine -- a deployment that he said would be a "continuation of war".

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were in Moscow after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi searching for a way to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II.

Putin's comments appeared to douse hopes that a deal to end the war could be within grasp, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there was a "window of opportunity" to achieve "a result" before 2027.

The Americans, meanwhile, urged Putin to allow European representatives to sit at the table for the next round of talks.

Moscow has successfully managed to reframe the discussions on the war as part of a wider discussion about European security.

But Kyiv and European leaders have urged against a new "Yalta" -- a reference to the post-WWII deal to carve the continent into spheres of influence -- and said talks must be focused on ending the Ukraine war first.

Kushner and Witkoff will travel to Dublin, where a European summit is taking place, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky later on Thursday.

Usually held behind closed doors, the Kremlin chose to televise a lengthy opening exchange between Putin and the US envoys.

The Russian leader rejected talk of a possible territorial settlement involving "grey" -- or demilitarised -- zones between Ukrainian and Russian positions.

"For us, there is only one line of demarcation: the state border. Because then it will be clear and obvious: here are we, and here are you," he said.

Russia has seized swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine since launching its full-scale offensive in 2022. That is in addition to Crimea, which it annexed in 2014, and territory that was under the control of Russian-backed separatists.

Moscow has formally annexed four regions of Ukraine -- Donetsk, Kherson, Lugansk and Zaporizhzhia -- despite not having full control over them.

The annexations are rejected by Kyiv and the West as illegal and not recognised by the international community.

Advances by Russia's army have slowed throughout 2026 and hundreds of thousands have been killed in the almost five-year conflict, with millions more forced to flee their homes.

Putin proposed organising what he called a "humanitarian mission" to the frontline city of Kostyantynivka, where he said some 400-500 civilians still lived.

Russia claimed in the summer to have captured the city, but Ukraine insists fighting is ongoing for control.

The idea would be modelled on a short-term truce that last month allowed hundreds of stranded and starving locals to flee the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.

Putin also repeated his long-standing objection to any foreign troops being deployed to Ukraine as a post-war peacekeeping force -- something Kyiv says is crucial to thwarting another Russian attack.

Moscow would see any foreign troops deployed in the country as a "legitimate target," Putin said, adding their deployment would be a "vicious circle" and mean "the continuation of war".

European countries have been rattled by Russia pushing a review of the entire continent's security architecture, with the US also floating a new framework.

That is widely seen as a reference to Moscow's long-standing demands to push back the NATO military alliance in eastern Europe and end Western military support to Kyiv.

Some 50 European leaders gathered in the Irish capital Thursday, where EU chief Antonio Costa said "there is no need to reinvent the wheel" on Europe's security framework as he accused Russia of wrecking it by attacking Ukraine.

French President Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Europe to rally behind a "clear and united vision" on what it wants from Ukraine talks.

Russia and the United States are pushing Europe to name a single representative who they can deal with.

Amid the talks, the death and destruction continued.

Overnight, Russian strikes hit a residential building in Kyiv, killing one person.

In Putin's home city of Saint Petersburg, a car bomb blast killed a Russian soldier -- the latest in a string of apparent assassinations of military figures inside Russia.

Zelensky also reported fresh restrictions had been placed on the Starshield satellite internet service, key to Ukraine's front line communications.

articles.title: At least five people shot, one killed, in central Washington, DC
articles.summary: Authorities say the suspected shooter has been apprehended, after he shot himself.
articles.body:
Police have apprehended a gunman who allegedly shot five people, killing one, in a busy thoroughfare in the centre of Washington, DC on Thursday morning.

Interim Police Chief Jeffery Carroll said the suspect, a white male, then barricaded himself inside a nearby apartment building. Police were negotiating with the suspect on the phone when they heard gunshots. Upon entering the room, they found the man had shot himself, Carrol said.

The shooting occurred on Thursday near Logan Circle, at the intersection of 15th Street NW and P Street, police said, at 8:23am local time (13:28 GMT).

Local and federal law enforcement, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Secret Service, cordoned off the area and worked to apprehend the suspected gunman, said Al Jazeera’s John Holman, reporting from the scene.

A witness told The Associated Press news agency he saw one person shot in the head inside a gym at the scene.

James Spellman was at the gym when he heard shots being fired. He said there were about 50 people there at the time.

“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” he said. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”

Spellman said he and other gym members ran out of the gym and he heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.

The attack took place about 1.6km (one mile) from the White House during the rush hour commute.

Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown. Police issued a shelter-in-place order as law enforcement descended on the block.

“Go inside the nearest building, stay away from windows, and remain indoors until further notice,” police instructed the public. Trump’s focus on crime

The attack comes as the administration of United States President Donald Trump has made crime in the US capital a key issue during his second term.

That has included deploying the US National Guard across the city, a move Trump took after a former Department of Government Efficiency official said he was assaulted in the early hours of a morning in August 2025.

The US president declared a crime emergency, which also included federalising control of the federal district’s local police force.

Several thousand National Guard troops have remained in the district, with Trump regularly claiming their presence has brought down crime . Local officials have said the National Guard has not been used in local law enforcement.

The presence of the soldiers has at times caused friction with local officials, including Washington, DC mayor Muriel Bowser.

Speaking at a press conference alongside the police chief after the shooting, Bowser praised local police for their quick response to the incident, and dismissed the suggestion law enforcement had treated it with unusual importance.

“I praise [DC police] for bringing down crime in this city, and I praise our prosecutors,” Bowser said. “It’s not typical to have a active shooter that guns down people in the city, so all our law enforcement responded.”

The White House did not immediately comment on Thursday’s attack.

In November of last year, a National Guard member was killed by a gunman while on duty near 17th and I Streets NW. A second National Guard member was wounded.

In October, another National Guard member was shot during a gunfight in southeast Washington, DC.

Local law enforcement respond to reports of an active shooter in Washington, DC, the US [Tom Brenner/AP]

articles.title: Trump heads to China amid Nvidia scandal: Will he get tougher on Beijing?
articles.summary: Outgoing Nvidia chief credited with easing US-China chip ties but personal scandal unlikely to upend next week’s talks.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump travels to the Chinese city of Shenzhen next week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where he is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The trip comes as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s outgoing chief executive and one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley, faces mounting scrutiny over his relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence . China has denied the allegations.

On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang would step down as chief executive.

Huang accompanied Trump on his May visit to Beijing .

His presence mattered for Nvidia, which has struggled to secure approval to sell its H200 AI chips in China. Now, his place in the next delegation is in doubt.

So could Trump’s closeness to Huang push his administration towards a tougher line on China? Here’s what you need to know:

How did Huang shape the US-China chip thaw?

As founder and CEO of Nvidia, Huang pushed Washington to ease restrictions on the sale of advanced chips to China, arguing that wider use of US technology would help Washington hold onto its lead in AI development.

In December 2025, Trump did approve sales of the H200, Nvidia’s second-most powerful chip, to China, with 25 percent of proceeds to be paid to the US government.

He did so despite opposition from China hawks in both parties.

Huang was a surprise late addition to Trump’s delegation to Beijing in May, in hopes of unlocking stalled H200 sales. Despite Trump’s decision to allow the sales, shipments were low because of slow import approvals from the Chinese government in a bid to support domestic chipmakers.

Trump has stood by Huang throughout his recent personal scandal, calling him an “honourable guy”.

Will the Nvidia scandal prompt Trump to take a tougher stance with China?

Huang’s removal from Nvidia’s board and the scandal leading up to that are unlikely to significantly affect relations between Washington and Beijing, which Steve Okun, a Singapore-based geopolitical analyst, told Al Jazeera is “a stalemate at best”.

Instead, if the US continues to impose restrictions on AI product sales to China, AI diversion and diffusion – how products are traded around the world both formally and informally – would be much more likely to cause tension between the two nations.

Gabriel Wildau, managing director at the advisory firm Teneo, told Al Jazeera earlier this week that Trump “shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement”.

But he warned that the president “may face new pressure from Congress and hawkish voices inside his administration”.

Carsten Holz, an expert on the Chinese economy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, said Trump “would not seem to have a coherent China policy and therefore his position in the upcoming talks in Shenzhen is hard to predict”.

Huang’s personal affairs “will be of little relevance” to China-US relations, he told Al Jazeera.

Where is the pressure to be tougher with China coming from?

Mostly from Congress, where control of both houses will pass to the Democrats in January.

Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at the technology research group Omdia, said a tough US line on AI and China was not Trump’s alone, calling it “one of the rare political consensuses domestically across the aisle”.

Trump, he said, “will do whatever he can to protect his contribution and legacy on this matter”.

On Wednesday, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve all records on Nvidia’s chip exports to China.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

The news website Axios reported that Lutnick had held up a planned crackdown on firms suspected of funnelling Nvidia chips to China.

Meanwhile, procurement notices seen by the AFP news agency show that a Chinese university linked to the country’s defence establishment bought Nvidia H200 chips through a third party in September and October.

Beijing has rejected the spy claims and accused Washington of using them as cover to impose stronger restrictions and semiconductor export controls on China.

“The US side should stop fabricating such ‘spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning said on Thursday.

But Mao also said China is willing to work with the US to implement the consensus reached by the two leaders.

Omdia’s Su said China “has no interest in not engaging with Trump, given substantial interest in Nvidia graphics processing units”.

Chinese chipmakers may also gain from better access to US technology.

Shares in Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon, China’s leading makers of graphics processors, jumped nearly 10 percent on Thursday.

Holz, the Chinese economy expert, noted that the use of advanced Nvidia chips in Singapore data centres to serve customers in mainland China was “not new information”.

Still, Okun expects the pressure to build next year.

He said Congress could pass the Remote Access Security Act , aimed at stopping Chinese firms from reaching advanced chips through the cloud.

The Department of Commerce, he added, could put export controls on Megaspeed or require licences for advanced chips sent to countries such as Singapore and Malaysia.

If that happens, it will strain the US-China relationship in 2027, he said, adding “but that’s not going to happen next week”.

images.caption: US President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after presenting him with the National Medal of Science, in Washington, DC, US, October 8, 2026 [Evan Vucci/Reuters]
US President Donald Trump, right, and Chinese President Xi Jinping leave Zhongnanhai Garden on May 15, 2026 in Beijing, China [File: Evan Vucci/Pool via Getty Images]

articles.title: Texas Democrats put DEI back on agenda after sweeping to power
articles.summary: Texas Dems introduced bills to repeal a 2023 law banning DEI at universities across Texas, reigniting an an uncertain future for the controversial programs in the state.
articles.body: Texas Democrats are opening their incoming state House majority with a push to clear the way for DEI offices and programs to return to public universities across the state — a move state Republicans are expected to block but that puts the culture-war issue front and center after massive Democratic Party gains in the state. HB 358 and SB 125 would repeal a 2023 law banning diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) offices and programs at public universities, but the bills face steep odds with Republicans still retaining control of the Texas Senate. Still, the effort signals Democrats’ broader intent to roll back one of the GOP’s signature education policies after campaigning heavily on the war in Iran, immigration and affordability. Even if the repeal effort fails, conservative policy experts in Texas warn that Democratic appointments to university governing boards could weaken enforcement of the state's DEI restrictions without changing the law. "With Republicans in firm control of the Texas state Senate, it’s highly unlikely that any bill seeking to bring back the corrosive and wasteful higher ed DEI regime will make it to the Governor’s desk," Chuck DeVore, chief national initiatives officer for the Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF), told Fox News Digital. "What will likely happen is that relabeled and disguised DEI programs and classes will make a comeback over the next four years as the Governor’s board of regents appointees gradually get a majority. We look forward to suing to ensure adherence to Texas law." FEDERAL JUDGE KICKED OFF 'BOTCH JOB' ANTI-DEI CASE AFTER STUNNING APPEALS COURT REBUKE The 2023 anti-DEI law, signed by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, barred public universities from maintaining DEI offices or assigning employees or contractors to perform their duties. It also prohibited compelling or soliciting DEI statements from faculty or students, restricted certain preferences based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin and banned mandatory DEI training for students and employees. The law includes exceptions for academic instruction, scholarly research and registered student organizations. After the law took effect Jan. 1, 2024, UT Austin closed its Multicultural Engagement Center and discontinued its Monarch program, which provided advising, mental-health support and scholarships to illegal immigrants and other noncitizen students. The University of Houston System stopped requiring DEI statements in hiring and promotions, while UT Health San Antonio ended a faculty loan-repayment program for professors from "underrepresented backgrounds." VP VANCE TOUTS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S DISMANTLING OF DEI At a May 2024 Texas Senate higher education subcommittee hearing, UT System Chancellor J.B. Milliken told lawmakers the system had closed 21 DEI offices, eliminated 311 full- and part-time positions focused on DEI and canceled 681 contracts, programs and training sessions. Critics have nevertheless accused some universities of preserving DEI initiatives under different names or organizational structures. Texas A&M University drew scrutiny after dissolving its Office for Diversity but transferring six of its eight employees to other campus positions. Former Vice President for Diversity Annie McGowan received a 10% raise, a new position and nine months of paid leave. Critics accused the university of preserving DEI operations under different titles. Texas A&M maintained that the office and its DEI-related duties had been eliminated and that the raises were unrelated to DEI. Kate Bierly, a higher education campaign director at TPPF, told Fox News Digital that Democrats could undermine Texas' 2023 anti-DEI law without repealing it. She warned that newly appointed university regents could weaken enforcement through administrative inaction, potentially allowing prohibited practices to resume. She observed that numerous university regents' terms expire Feb. 1, 2027, giving Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa an opportunity to nominate replacements who could influence how universities enforce the DEI ban. CONGRESS TO PUT AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION IN HOT SEAT OVER DEI RULES TIED TO LAW SCHOOL ACCREDITATION But Hinojosa would face another obstacle: Republican control of the Texas Senate, which must confirm university regent appointments. Bierly said the Texas Constitution allows certain unpaid gubernatorial appointees, including regents, to remain in office after their terms expire. Because the 90th Legislature convenes in January 2027, before the regents' terms expire, she said incumbents could remain in place until the end of the 91st Legislature's regular session in 2029 if their successors are not confirmed. "If the Senate declines to confirm nominees who would undermine the state's DEI reforms, existing regents can continue serving rather than automatically surrendering their seats when their terms expire," Bierly said. "This holdover period ends on the last day of the first regular legislative session that begins after the term expires. So as a result, the current regents can hold over to 2029 if no successor has qualified by then. After that, the office becomes vacated." DeVore said the holdover provision could become a political liability for Senate Republicans, giving Democrats "an actual useful campaign cudgel" if the chamber refuses to confirm Hinojosa's nominees. Democrats could accuse Republicans of obstructing the governor's appointments to university governing boards, he said. That pressure could force a compromise at some point, DeVore added, but also warned that DEI is "a death issue for a Republican primary" and that any Republican who supports a compromise could be "toast in the primary." DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR Texas' restrictions reflect a broader national effort to dismantle DEI programs in government and higher education. The Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling against race-based admissions preferences at universities preceded a broader federal crackdown on DEI. After returning to office in 2025, President Donald Trump moved to dismantle DEI programs across the federal government and directed federally funded schools to end race-based preferences in admissions, hiring, scholarships and other programs. Republican-led states have pursued similar restrictions at public universities, making Texas’ fight part of a broader national backlash against institutional DEI. Texas' political landscape has shifted dramatically following Republican election losses. Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and Attorney General Ken Paxton are leaving office, while Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, lost his Republican Senate primary to Paxton. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Democrats won the governorship, attorney general's office and a U.S. Senate seat while reclaiming the state House for the first time in more than two decades. Republicans retained control of the state Senate, giving them a potential veto over both the DEI repeal legislation and Hinojosa's university regent nominees. "Ultimately, Texas lawmakers must decide whether they want the DEI ban to be more than a law on paper," Bierly said. "Protecting the reforms requires attention not only to legislation, but also to the university leadership responsible for implementing it." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Fox News Digital sought comment from the repeal bills' sponsors, Democratic state Rep. John Bucy and Democratic state Sen. José Menéndez, as well as former Republican state Sen. Brandon Creighton, who authored the 2023 anti-DEI law and now serves as chancellor of the Texas Tech University System. None responded before publication. The University of Texas System, Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board and Texas Students for DEI also did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Pence delivers scathing rebuke of Vance's Iran war assessment, blames Trump policies for GOP losses
articles.summary: Mike Pence rejects JD Vance's claim that the Iran war alone cost Republicans Congress, pointing to inflation, self-dealing and policy failures.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE - Former Vice President Mike Pence delivered a blistering assessment of Vice President JD Vance's midterm election postmortem that the war in Iran cost Republicans control of Congress, with the former vice president contending that Americans grew frustrated not because President Donald Trump launched the conflict, but because his administration failed to finish it. Pence, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, his first following the midterms, also took aim at the vice president’s statements on Israel, saying he has "great concerns about what I’ve heard coming out of the vice president’s office with regard to Israel." Asked about Vance's assessment, Pence said, "I disagree with the vice president about the reasons for the midterm election outcome." "There's no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn't because President Trump started the war or took on Iran. It's because we stopped short and didn't finish it," Pence said. "As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump." RUBIO'S DEFENSE OF TRUMP'S IRAN WAR DRAWS SHARP CONTRAST WITH VANCE'S MIDTERM BLAME But the former vice president emphasized "the reasons for this midterm election were much more complex than gasoline prices or the war in Iran. So, I respectfully disagree with my successor in that regard." "If the world knows nothing else, the world should know that America stands with Israel. Israel is our most cherished ally. It is the only democracy in the Arab world," Pence a longtime strong supporter of Israel, emphasized. Pence said he's "very troubled at the way that criticism of Israel on the left and on the right collapses too often into antisemitism and antisemitic rhetoric. There's no place in America for antisemitism on the left or on the right and the people that are wringing their hands about U.S. support for Israel, I get the feeling sometimes they're just using that as a thinly veiled excuse for their antisemitism." ‘HE BLAMED THE JEWS’: GOP CONGRESSMAN LEVELS EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATION AGAINST JD VANCE OVER ELECTION POSTMORTEM Vance, in an assessment the morning after Election Day, wrote, "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night." The vice president also cited an unnamed pollster in his X post who said voters who had abandoned the GOP wanted the administration to end the conflict, address inflation and the cost of living, put America first and change its relationship with Israel. A Vance ally, responding to Pence's criticism, told Fox News Digital, "Former Vice President Pence had to retreat into the think tank world because his politics never developed past the Bush-era neocon warmongering that dragged us into the Middle East in the first place. He is laughably out of touch with how people feel in the real world." VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS Pence, who served as vice president in Trump's first term, pointed to the president's second term tariffs, the administration's handling of abortion medication and the first family's growing wealth as factors in the GOP's electoral defeat, arguing that Republicans must return to traditional conservative principles to reclaim their congressional majorities. While the high cost of living and the war in Iran were key issues in the midterms, the Fox News Voter Poll also highlighted that 55% of respondents said government corruption was a "crucial" factor in their vote for Congress, with another 36% saying it was a major factor. Pence argued that "I don't think you can ignore the air of corruption that's emerged around this administration, the self-dealing. ARMY SECRETARY DAN DRISCOLL SUBMITS RESIGNATION TO TRUMP Fort McNair's residential quarters are divided into two housing groups, according to a 2020 National Capital Planning Commission report, while a 2024 Army filing identifies 27 historic homes built before 1919 at the installation. articles.title: AOC taps power player who helped Bernie Sanders defy the odds as major 2028 decision looms
articles.summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tapped the strategist behind Bernie Sanders' record-breaking fundraising as progressive groups push her toward a 2028 bid.
articles.body: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is tapping a key player behind Bernie Sanders' presidential fundraising operation as speculation swirls over whether the left-wing Democrat could launch her own White House bid in 2028. Ocasio-Cortez split with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, Axios reported Thursday, citing three sources familiar with the matter. She has now tapped Aisle 518 Strategies, the firm led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who helped drive Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising operations during his 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, according to Axios. The move comes as some progressive groups are calling for Ocasio-Cortez to jump into the White House race in 2028. There has also been mounting speculation that she could seek the Senate seat held by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in 2028, potentially setting up a Democratic primary showdown if Schumer seeks re-election. AOC CAMPAIGN MEMO FRAMES GROWTH FROM PROGRESSIVE FIREBRAND TO NATIONAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY FORCE Ocasio-Cortez's office declined to comment to Fox News Digital on Thursday. Middle Seat and Aisle 518 Strategies each did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests seeking comment. Sanders' 2016 fundraising operation capitalized on major campaign moments and attacks from establishment Democrats to generate surges in small-dollar donations, helping propel the relatively obscure Vermont senator into an unexpectedly competitive primary battle against Hillary Clinton, Politico reported at the time. "Internet fundraising is about taking potential energy and converting it into kinetic energy, and nobody has done that better than Bernie Sanders," veteran Democratic operative Ari Rabin-Havt told Politico back in 2016. "Tim [Tagaris] and his team are maximizing that. Their emails are superior." Sanders' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Sanders' campaign raised $34.5 million in the final three months of 2019, according to the AP. He went on to briefly emerge as the Democratic front-runner in early 2020 before Joe Biden consolidated support and secured the nomination. articles.title: Biden judge rejects DOJ bid to halt probe of prosecutors in botched ICE protest case
articles.summary: Judge April Perry ordered U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros and three prosecutors to give sworn testimony in the Broadview Six case amid misconduct allegations.
articles.body: A federal judge investigating whether prosecutors misled her court in the "Broadview Six" case against anti-ICE protesters canceled a hearing requested by the Justice Department to clarify her authority to conduct the inquiry. U.S. District Judge April Perry, a Biden appointee, has ordered four federal prosecutors, including Chicago's U.S. attorney, to testify under oath as she considers possible sanctions or criminal contempt proceedings. "Ultimately, the Government’s professed lack of clarity about the Court’s inherent authority to ask lawyers who have made misstatements to or misled the Court to explain their actions is immaterial," Perry wrote Wednesday, canceling the Nov. 17 hearing. The Justice Department dropped the criminal case against the six protesters in May amid allegations of misconduct involving former federal prosecutor Sheri Mecklenburg, who later resigned. But Perry's investigation into the prosecutors' conduct has continued. DOJ MOVES TO BOOT FEDERAL JUDGES FROM IMMIGRATION CASES OVER NYT INTERVIEW Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the Justice Department's third-ranking official, argued in a filing that requiring prosecutors to testify would put them in a "Catch-22." "They can testify and risk prosecution, or they can assert their rights under the Fifth Amendment and risk antagonizing the court, while it may also be considering non-contempt sanctions," Woodward wrote. Perry rejected the government's argument, writing that "the Government does not represent at least 3/4 of the individuals who have been asked to testify, two of whom have expressed their willingness to do so." Perry has ordered U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros and three assistant U.S. attorneys in the Northern District of Illinois — William Hogan, Matthew Skiba and Andres Almendarez — to testify under oath Monday about possible misconduct in grand jury proceedings involving the protesters. "There is no indication on the docket that the Government represents the fourth individual," Perry wrote, referring to Boutros. The testimony is expected to address prosecutors' knowledge of possible grand jury misconduct, the accuracy of their statements to the court, why grand jury transcripts were redacted and whether officials outside the U.S. Attorney's Office received information about the investigation. Perry could use the testimony to determine whether sanctions or criminal contempt proceedings are warranted. DOJ MOVES TO BOOT TWO FEDERAL JUDGES FROM IMMIGRATION CASES OVER REMARKS TO MEDIA: 'EXTRAORDINARILY IMPRUDENT' The canceled hearing follows a separate dispute over communications the Justice Department has declined to disclose to Perry. On Monday, Woodward argued in a motion that certain communications involving federal prosecutors were privileged and should not be disclosed. The Justice Department also submitted a privilege log identifying the withheld communications and the grounds for withholding them. Perry rejected the submission Tuesday, finding it "noncompliant" because the government had redacted information identifying numerous senders and recipients in lengthy email chains. She also questioned the Justice Department's response to her request for an email sent to Boutros containing an expedited transcript of the Oct. 9, 2025, grand jury session, when jurors first declined to return an indictment. The PDF, the judge said, lacked metadata that could help establish whether Boutros had read the email. Prosecutors were given until Thursday to address her concerns. The inquiry began May 20, when Perry ordered prosecutors involved in redacting grand jury transcripts to appear in court and questioned them during a sealed hearing the following day. ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS CLASH WITH AGENTS OUTSIDE NEW JERSEY DETENTION CENTER AS GOV SHERRILL DENIED ENTRY In October, Perry requested communications between federal prosecutors and outside officials concerning investigative and charging decisions in the case, finding that "several aspects of this prosecution were very flawed." The inquiry stems from a grand jury's refusal to return an indictment on Oct. 9, 2025, and again during a subsequent session convened by Boutros, when two jurors were excused over concerns about their impartiality. Those jurors later returned for a third session on Oct. 23, when the grand jury indicted the protesters on a felony conspiracy charge. According to court records, grand jury transcripts initially provided to Perry in April contained redactions that concealed evidence of possible misconduct, including allegations of improper "vouching" for the government's case by former Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri Mecklenburg during an Oct. 9, 2025, grand jury presentation. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Six protesters, including former Democratic congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, faced federal charges stemming from a Sept. 26, 2025, confrontation outside an ICE facility in Broadview, Illinois. Prosecutors alleged that the demonstrators surrounded a federal immigration agent's vehicle to prevent him from entering the facility. Members of the crowd allegedly struck the vehicle, damaging a side mirror and windshield wiper, although prosecutors did not identify any of the six defendants as personally responsible. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The other defendants were Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, Chicago Democratic Committeeman Michael Rabbitt, Abughazaleh campaign staffer Andre Martin, former Cook County Board candidate Catherine Sharp and musician Joselyn Walsh.

articles.title: WATCH: Socialist agitators lose it when cameras turn on them
articles.summary: CodePink and Singham-linked activists swarmed Congress on Veterans Day, but when cameras turned on them, they blocked lenses and hurled insults.
articles.body: WASHINGTON, D.C. — Far-left activists from the network funded by communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham can dish it out, but they can't take it. For years, CodePink activists, easily recognizable in hot pink T-shirts, have heckled lawmakers and officials in public settings with a tactic called "bird dogging," cornering targets, peppering them with hostile questions, like "Why do you support baby killers?" and shaming them on social media with tactics that amount to humiliation rituals. On Veterans Day, the agitators found themselves on the other side of the lens, and they didn't like it. For six hours on Wednesday, Fox News Digital followed members of CodePink, BreakThrough News, the People's Forum, the Party for Socialism and Liberation and allied groups in the Singham network through the halls of Congress during a lobbying event organizers called the "Taxpayer Uprising." But when the cameras turned on them, they angrily refused to answer questions and covered the camera lens, one time with a Palestinian keffiyeh scarf and another time with a backpack designed with the pattern of a watermelon, a symbol adopted by the Palestinian movement. Then, they responded with smears and ad hominem attacks. Finally, they published their footage of the confrontations, turning their objections to being filmed into content for their followers. One follower congratulated them on their success deploying "psychic militancy." LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION Breakfast with Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y. The day began just before 10 a.m. inside the Rayburn House Office Building, where activists in pink CodePink T-shirts and keffiyehs walked into a breakfast gathering of the U.S. House Bagel Caucus. At 9:59 a.m., they surrounded Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., and pointed their cameras at him. Medea Benjamin, co-founder of CodePink, wore a shirt emblazoned with the message "NO WAR ON IRAN" and pressed him on Section 219 of the National Defense Authorization Act, which she called a "merging" of the U.S. and Israeli militaries. "It is not a merging of the militaries," Goldman said. "It is a collaboration on technology that we depend on Israel for, and they depend on us for, and it is for our own national security." He asked the activists whether they supported Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Hamas and Hezbollah. "We're not funding them. We're funding Israel," Benjamin replied. When the liberal congressman called the situation in Gaza "absolutely horrific" and said he wished Hamas would allow in the aid Israel was trying to send, the group members groaned in unison. CodePink activist Tighe Barry, Benjamin's husband, in a pink shirt and pink hat, yelled at him: "You're a real congressman, and you just made that statement?" "That was a horrific lie that you just said," Barry shouted at him. "As a sitting congressman, I take deep offense at that." "Alright, here we are. We're enjoying the Bagel Caucus here," Goldman said before walking away. "Thank you for talking. Take care of yourself." HOW CODEPINK CO-FOUNDER MEDEA BENJAMIN'S FAMILY FOUNDATION BECAME A MAJOR FUNDER OF LEFT-WING ACTIVIST GROUPS 'I'm sorry, I can't hear you' CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin moved through the building wearing a backpack designed with the pattern of a keffiyeh, the checkered scarf that has become a symbol of the pro-Palestinian movement. At 10:06 a.m., the group shuffled to the Rayburn cafeteria, where organizers had set up tables numbered by lobbying group. Pink signs reading "TAXPAYER UPRISING" and "WAR IS NOT GREEN" sat on the tables. Confrontations began within minutes. "No, no. Hey, out of here," a CodePink volunteer told the reporter at about 10:09 a.m. Asked for an interview, Barry turned to his fellow activists and balked, saying, "Why would I?" AS SINGHAM FACES FEDERAL PROBE, WIFE MARCHES IN ANTI-ISRAEL PROTEST LED BY GROUPS HE FUNDED A woman at the check-in table asked the reporter to "move your camera away." Another activist used a keffiyeh to block the camera's view, and a Muslim woman in a headscarf put her hand over the lens. At about 10:12 a.m., an activist hoisted a pink backpack printed with watermelons in front of the Fox News Digital camera. A young man in a keffiyeh, with a name tag that read "Finn," then planted himself in front of the camera and moved with it as it tried to pan around him. "Is this what you do in your free time, is like, wander around?" he taunted. Melissa Garriga, CodePink's media contact, refused to answer any questions, priding herself to the team on refusing to answer emailed requests for comment from Fox News Digital. Asked a question by the reporter standing right in front of her, she cupped her hand behind her ear and said, "I'm sorry, I can't hear you. Can you speak up?" Asked again, she responded, "I still can't hear you. You're gonna have to talk a little louder. Sorry." Then, again: "Can you please speak up?" Asked about Singham's funding of CodePink, Garriga waved her hand across the lens. "I don't have to respond to you," she said. At 10:14 a.m., Garriga put her hand fully over the camera: "Just buzz off," she said. The activist with the "Finn" name tag returned and held a gray jacket over the lens, then a canvas tote bag, then a keffiyeh, one after another. Minutes later, a red-haired woman in a keffiyeh waved her hands in front of the camera. 'They work for us' Shortly after 10:20 a.m., CodePink co-founders Jodie Evans and Benjamin took charge of the room. Evans married Singham in 2017 when he sold his company, Thoughtworks, for an estimated $785 million. He used some of those proceeds to pump $285 million into a network of nonprofits that have been pro-China and pro-communist. Several of their leaders hit the halls of Congress on Wednesday. "Alright, everybody, we want to start our program," Evans said at 10:22 a.m. Benjamin urged them to confront lawmakers wherever they found them. "Remember, they work for us. They're not better than us. They are public servants," she said. "And so, if you see them, try to engage them." She told the activists how to spot members of Congress in the hallways: They wear lapel pins and aren't holding anything, because staff carry documents, binders and other items for them, she said. "The worst it could be is they say, 'I'm not a congressperson,'" she said. Singham has denied acting at the direction of the Chinese government. Asked if her husband would do an interview, Evans, the only member of the entourage to respond professionally to questions, smiled and said, "No, he's shy." Fresh from a propaganda tour to China, the Singham network activists pressed lawmakers to slash the military budget, pull out U.S. troops and end U.S. military ties with Israel — demands that align with China's foreign policy agenda. Rania Khalek, a co-host of "BT Live" at BreakThrough News, slipped into the cafeteria. When Fox News Digital asked Khalek about BreakThrough's funding from Singham, she responded, "Oh dear. I'm not speaking to you." A man in a pink shirt stepped backward to plant himself in front of the camera. Khalek raised her phone, filmed the reporter and asked, "Are you harassing us?" She then answered her own question: "Yes." Asked whether she was with the Party for Socialism and Liberation, a woman standing with Khalek smiled and replied, "Am I?" She has led Party for Socialism and Liberation protests at the White House and is a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation. At 10:26 a.m., two activists stepped in front of the camera at once and another pushed a cafeteria chair into the reporter's path. At 10:33 a.m., Khalek walked behind Benjamin and Evans with the activist from the Party for Socialism and Liberation to hit offices. Outside Hakeem Jeffries' office By 10:35 a.m., the activists had moved to the second floor of the Rayburn building, where U.S. Capitol Police officers stood outside Room 2267, the office of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. A yellow sign taped inside the office door read, "OFFICE CLEARED." The activists only met with a staffer. At 11:11 a.m., Benjamin did a stand-up video in front of Jeffries' door, casting the image of a dramatic confrontation between activists who "packed" the small office foyer and Jeffries. 'Nobody cares what you think' At 11:20 a.m., Khalek exploded. Near the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, "The fact that you pretend to care about free speech right now while literal journalists in Gaza are being, like, executed, sniped in the head by the IDF with U.S. weapons, is a freaking joke. Okay? Nobody cares what you think." Holding up her phone, she added, "I'm literally doing journalism right now. See?" Asked whether it was acceptable for Singham network activists to disrupt congressional hearings, Khalek answered with a question of her own: "Is it okay to fund genocide?" Then she walked away. At 11:22 a.m., she lashed out, calling the reporter a "genocide apologist." Another activist stepped in front of the camera and took over. "Shame on you. You're completely shameless," she said. "You are a disgrace to this profession!" The Party for Socialism and Liberation activist filmed the exchange with Khalek. BreakThrough News later posted the confrontation on Instagram and X, quoting Khalek, who lives in Lebanon, saying: "Stop justifying bombing my country!" One follower praised the outburst as "psychic militancy." Her outburst over, Khalek proceeded to go chase lawmakers. At 11:25 a.m., a woman in a pink CodePink shirt draped a keffiyeh over the camera lens, then followed the reporter and raised it onto the lens again. Olivia DiNucci, CodePink's D.C. coordinator, wore an olive jacket that read "STOP ARMING ISRAEL." DiNucci has heckled Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Palantir CEO Alex Karp and scores of others, and has written first-person accounts of her own arrests and disruptions inside Congress. On Wednesday, she threw her hand in front of the camera. "We just don't wanna talk to you, because you're complicit in genocide," she yelled. "Is that really hard for you to understand?" She continued: "We're not interested in talking to people who support murdering babies." At 11:34 a.m., Benjamin, Khalek and the Party for Socialism and Liberation activist intercepted a congressman walking past the Rayburn House Office Building sign, pressing him on the activists' demands. "That's propaganda," he responded. Scalise: 'Maybe there's another country that they like better' By lobbying day's end, at 3:28 p.m., on the steps of the U.S. Capitol, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., spoke to Fox News Digital, as the activists stood with their signs, cordoned away behind police barricades. Their signs read "WELCOME TO DC / LET'S END WAR" and "HEALTHCARE NOT WARFARE." "Some people like yelling and screaming and making a lot of noise," Scalise said. "They sure do want attention focused on them so people can see how radical they are. And some of these people are just against the foundations of what made this nation great." "We're here at a Veterans Day ceremony of all things and they want to protest," he said. "Anybody who would protest Veterans Day, you know, they need to really check themselves. Maybe there's another country that they like better than America, they're free to go there. We love this country." Scalise added, "Ask Europe who liberated it. It was the United States with our allies that stopped the Nazis, stopped fascism, and we've always been the ones, America, standing up to the bad guys." "You just follow the money when you see who funds some of these groups that hate America," he said. "It tells you everything you need to know." Follow the money The money behind the groups involved in the lobbying day is substantial. According to IRS filings, Singham has given $1.098 million to BreakThrough's BT Media Inc., $1.33 million to CodePink and $22.44 million to The People's Forum. CodePink lists 56 organizations taking part in the Taxpayer Uprising with an estimated $40 million in annual revenues, according to Fox News Digital's investigation. The coalition includes the Council on American-Islamic Relations, American Muslims for Palestine, the Democratic Socialists of America's International Committee and the Communist Party USA, which says on its website that it "is guided by Marxism-Leninism." Other participants describe themselves in socialist terms, including Friends of Socialist China, which calls itself "a platform based on supporting the People's Republic of China and promoting understanding of Chinese socialism," and Qiao Collective, which says it is "committed to the principles of socialist internationalism." They're not grassroots groups. They have big revenue totals: CAIR Foundation at $9.4 million, the People's Forum at $7.1 million, the Institute for Policy Studies at $5.7 million, Nonviolence International at $3.7 million, Global Exchange at $3 million, American Muslims for Palestine's AJP Educational Foundation at $2.1 million, CodePink at $1.8 million and BreakThrough at $1.5 million. Fox News Digital couldn't identify any group registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, according to the Justice Department's FARA database. Last year, Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., wrote a letter raising concerns about CodePink's pro-China lobbying. Rubio has pressed the Justice Department about Chinese Communist Party information warfare through these nonprofits. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., has sent subpoenas to the People's Forum, BreakThrough News and a related Tricontinental thinktank as allegedly aligned with the Chinese Communist Party propaganda operation. Overnight, CodePink posted the video where she spoke to her team's camera in front of Jeffries' office, with the caption, telling the world: "We just packed the office of Hakeem Jeffries." articles.title: Washington DC shooting leaves one dead, four injured as suspect dies after standoff
articles.summary: One victim is in a critical condition and three others have non life-threatening injuries, officials say.
articles.body:
One person has been killed and four others injured after a gunman opened fire in Washington DC.

The shooting began on Thursday morning local time inside a gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle neighbourhood, which is about a mile (1.6km) north of the White House.

Police said the male suspect was "contained" after barricading himself in one of the apartments. They later confirmed he had died.

Of those injured, one is in a critical condition and the others have non-life-threatening injuries.

While the suspect was barricaded, "he did fire through the door at officers at least on two occasions", Jefferey Carroll, the interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department, said at a news conference.

Negotiators had been on the phone with the suspect when they heard a gunshot and he stopped communicating with them, according to Carroll.

Officers forced their way into the apartment and saw the suspect had what appeared to be a "self-inflicted gunshot wound", he said.

Carroll added that police "believe there was a fire that was set", which has been contained.

Authorities are still working to understand the exact timeline, suspect's motivation, and other details of the incident.

"We believe there was some sort of a conflict with the apartment building, but we don't have much more than that," Carroll said.

Washington DC Mayor Muriel Bowser called it a "senseless act of gun violence" and said the White House had been briefed.

A BBC producer who lives in the building where the shooting happened, Jonathan Csapo, said a fire alarm went off. Then, as he came out of a fire escape, he heard gunshots very close by.

"I could see the smoke, I could see the flash. We just all started running. That was our first instinct," he said.

"We immediately ran and took cover behind a barricade, a little brick structure just near the building."

Csapo said he was then taken back inside, to a safe room, by a building manager.

"And then everybody started screaming," he said.

Michael Carney told the Washington Sun he was on a treadmill at the Vida Fitness gym when the shooting started.

He says he heard "one pop" which he assumed was an exercise ball bursting before seeing a victim on the floor who had been shot.

"Everyone was kind of just hiding behind planters and stuff," he said, adding a fire alarm was pulled.

Once outside of the gym, Carney says he heard five or 10 shots that seemed to be coming from a nearby alley.

Another witness told the Washington Sun that she heard "an enormous, loud thing" in the fitness centre and more shots outside the gym after being evacuated.

"I thought something had crashed or fallen," she said. "I didn't know it was a gunshot until later."

articles.summary: VOX cerraría el podio (18,4%), seguido de Frente Amplio (4,7%)
articles.body: Estamos a tan solo 17 días de las elecciones generales (29N) y los partidos políticos continúan con su puesta en escena en los eventos de precampaña o con sus entrevistas en los diferentes medios de comunicación del país. Sin embargo, el barómetro del Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS) se actualiza cada diverso tiempo y el correspondiente a noviembre de 2026 ha salido a la luz y con novedades. Este último balance se llevó a cabo sobre una muestra de 45.074 personas y, tal y como apuntan los datos, el PSOE ganaría las elecciones generales en estos momentos con el 33,3% de los votos. Por su parte, el Partido Popular (PP) se quedaría en segunda posición con el 25,5%, mientras que VOX cerraría el podio con un 18,4%. Por detrás de ellos aparecería la nueva formación política, Frente Amplio, con un 4,7% de los votos y una estimación entre siete y 11 escaños. Por otro lado, ERC-Podemos llegaría hasta el 3,1% y podría lograr entre 10 y 14 diputados. Por su parte, EH Bildu estaría rondando el 2 % y se movería entre los siete y 10 representantes. Por otro lado, en lo que respecta a los escaños de las tres principales fuerzas políticas de España, el PSOE estaría entre los 134 y 143 diputados en el Congreso, mientras que los populares estarían entre 98 y 106 representantes y VOX entre 57 y 65. El resto de formaciones lograrían porcentajes más reducidos: Compromís-Front Valencià (1,6%, cuatro a seis escaños), Adelante Andalucía (1,5%, entre tres y cuatro), SALF (1,4%), Junts (1,2%), Podemos (1,1%),BNG (1%), EAJ-PNV (0,7%), UPC (0,4%) y Ara Més-Front Ampli (0,2%).
