articles.title: Trump opens door to immigration deal, but Republicans have one condition
articles.summary: President Donald Trump floated a deal for long-term immigrants, but Senate Republicans drew a hard line, insisting amnesty is completely off the table.
articles.body: Some Senate Republicans are open to revisiting immigration policy after President Donald Trump floated a possible deal with Democrats, but they insist amnesty remains off the table. Republicans, after sweeping midterm losses, are willing to open up the immigration policy debate after voters made clear that they didn't support the administration’s approach: a Fox News poll published in September found that 53% of voters believed that Trump's immigration policy had gone too far. But there’s one thing that Senate Republicans won’t agree to: amnesty. WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS "I trust President Trump," Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital. "He's gonna do what's right, but as far as I'm concerned, amnesty is off the table. I'll never go for it." The door creaked open on the idea when Trump, during an interview with "60 Minutes" that aired over the weekend, said that his administration’s mass deportation and enforcement policies might be "too tough." "Get the killers out, get the rapists out, get all the rough ones out, get the drug dealers out," Trump said. "But let the people that are here — and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years — work a deal for them." The administration quickly sought to clarify Trump’s comments, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin affirming that there would be "no amnesty" shortly after. HOUSE GOP ERUPTS AT STEPHEN MILLER AS TRUMP ELEVATES HIM AFTER MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'MEGALOMANIAC' Still, Republicans are willing to navigate the complex issue as Democrats gear up to take power next year. Some have been calling for action on the matter for months. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., one of the administration’s sharper Republican critics on immigration policy who is retiring at the end of the year, told Fox News Digital that as early as March he texted Trump and suggested it would be the "perfect time" to codify "all the stuff that has effectively sealed the border and used it as an opportunity to get merit-based immigration reform." "I also said in that text, though, was, in order for this to be successful, Stephen Miller either needs to be out of the room or on his meds," Tillis said. "And so he's the reason they're walking it back is because they don't want to do it, because they have some false assumption that that's gonna hurt our base." "Our base is fine with merit-based immigration reform. President Trump is fine with merit-based immigration reform," he continued. "And if we don't get the stuff codified that has effectively sealed the border, it's gonna be on them when the border gets opened up if a Democrat wins in ‘28." The Senate, just before Trump won the 2024 election, was on the cusp of a bipartisan immigration deal when Democrats controlled the chamber. The deal collapsed after Trump criticized it and Senate Republicans withdrew support. "There's a lot of scar tissue on this issue, but, you know, the president, because he secured the borders, he has credibility on the issue, and he has expressed a willingness," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "I have not seen anything yet that's being proposed, but we will certainly hear them out, and if there's something he wants to do there, have a conversation about it." JEFFRIES VOWS DEMOCRATS WON’T ‘GIVE A DIME’ TO TRUMP’S DEPORTATION EFFORTS The bipartisan deal was the product of negotiations among Sens. James Lankford, R-Okla., Chris Murphy, D-Conn., and former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema, and would have funneled billions for border security and shuttered the border to most asylum seekers, among several other policy changes. But conservatives balked at the deal, and Trump’s influence from the campaign trail ultimately killed it. Years later, Lankford is again in a prime position to work on a deal with Democrats, given that he is expected to become the ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee next year. "If I’m ranking on Homeland Security, I’m right in the thick of it, whether you like it or not," Lankford said. Though opinions vary on what exactly the GOP’s approach would be going forward, many Republicans agree that the administration’s enforcement policies, particularly under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, should not make a comeback. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think you have to make sure, first and foremost, that how you do your enforcement is not like the administration started under Kristi Noem," Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital. "I think people are for some enforcement, but not in a cruel way. And there were so many, there was a lack of training, lack of proper methodologies, and I think people want to take enforcement seriously." "But, again, I would say no amnesty at all," he continued. "We don't want to go there. Ronald Reagan, a great president, one of his few regrets, but significant regrets, was amnesty. And I don't think Trump wants to make that mistake."

articles.title: Howard Lutnick is next Trump official top Dems want on the chopping block amid NVIDIA scandal
articles.summary: Top House Democrats are calling for an investigation into Howard Lutnick over his alleged role in the NVIDIA Jensen Huang Chinese spy scandal.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE : Top House Democrats are calling for an investigation into Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over allegations involving NVIDIA's former CEO's reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang resigned this week following allegations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. In the midst of the spy scandal, multiple investigative reports emerged claiming Lutnick received a classified memo warning him about Huang’s relationship with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, of no familial relation to the NVIDIA CEO. "Howard Lutnick needs to be investigated over his role in Jensen Huang and the Chinese spy, we're going to have an investigation into those allegations, that's completely unacceptable," Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., who is expected to become chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, told Fox News Digital. FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL Lieu alleged that despite Lutnick being briefed on the reported relationship between Huang and a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy, he failed to take action. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., a vice chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and member of the House Select Committee on China, also expressed support for investigating Lutnick and did not rule out examining Secretary of State Marco Rubio's involvement, as well. "I think we need transparency," Khanna told Fox News Digital. "I think we need to understand what they knew." PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES "Rubio knew about the Chinese spy, and then got invited to the China trip," Khanna continued. "We need to get to the bottom of this." Lutnick and Rubio did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. REBECCA GRANT: JENSEN HUANG OWES AMERICA AN APOLOGY, AND NVIDIA OWES INVESTORS ANSWERS Many left-leaning lawmakers are jumping on the chance to name the Cabinet official they want to see face scrutiny when Democrats take back control of the House in January. However, neither Khanna or Lieu shed light on how they would investigate, prosecute or remove Lutnick, and potentially Rubio. Neither of the Cabinet secretaries have been formally accused or indicted of wrongdoing in connection with the NVIDIA case. House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is currently running unopposed for the Democratic nomination for Speaker of the House, did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on whether he spoke to either lawmakers on their desires to take action against Lutnick and Rubio. HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE The lawmakers' remarks signal that congressional Democrats could use their incoming majority to investigate senior Trump administration officials over their handling of alleged Chinese intelligence threats. It is unclear whether Republican lawmakers will support the Democrats' investigations. But following Huang’s resignation, House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., announced that the outgoing CEO has agreed to brief congressional committees following the scandal. He also advocated for Congress to act quickly to pass bipartisan export control legislation in the year-end national defense bill. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Moolenaar welcomed the resignation and added that companies such as NVIDIA should "never jeopardize our nation’s security by giving Chinese companies access to their most advanced chips," and called on them to "change its corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority."

articles.title: Trump asks Vance to focus on ‘corruption and crime’ in Dem-run cities, states
articles.summary: President Trump says JD Vance will target alleged corruption in Minnesota, California and Illinois, claiming billions are stolen monthly from government programs.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Thursday that he has asked Vice President JD Vance to focus his "complete and total attention" on alleged widespread corruption and crime in Democrat-led cities and states, accusing blue state leaders of allowing billions of dollars to be stolen each month. In a Truth Social post, Trump singled out Minnesota, California and Illinois as examples of states he claims are plagued by corruption and mismanagement, arguing that cracking down on the alleged criminal activity could help balance the federal budget. "I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.," Trump wrote. JD VANCE WARNS BLUE STATE OFFICIALS COULD FACE PRISON OVER BILLION-DOLLAR FRAUD EPIDEMIC "The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters," he continued. "Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month." Trump did not provide specific examples in his post of how billions of dollars are allegedly being stolen each month. Vance already leads the White House's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, which Trump established through a March 16 executive order aimed at combating fraud, waste and abuse in federally funded benefit programs. The task force is charged with coordinating federal efforts to strengthen eligibility verification, prevent improper payments and identify suspected fraud in government benefit programs. WALZ ADMINISTRATION IGNORED FRAUD WARNINGS AS BILLIONS VANISHED, HOUSE OVERSIGHT REPORT ALLEGES The executive order also identified Minnesota, California and Illinois among states where the administration alleged widespread fraud or vulnerabilities in government benefit programs. In October, Fox News Digital reported that the Vance-led task force was preparing to announce criminal charges against more than 40 defendants in an alleged $40 million Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) fraud scheme. At the time, the task force reported identifying $260.7 billion in suspected fraud since Trump took office and preventing an estimated $72 billion in potentially fraudulent payments on an annualized basis. Those figures have not been independently verified. It was not immediately clear whether Trump's latest directive would expand Vance's existing responsibilities or signal a renewed emphasis on investigating alleged corruption in Democratic-led jurisdictions. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Department of Justice for comment on the president's directive and the allegations of widespread fraud. Trump also suggested that eliminating the alleged corruption could help balance the federal budget. VANCE-LED TASK FORCE CUTS OFF $1.4B FROM HOME HEALTH, HOSPICE PROVIDERS SUSPECTED OF FRAUD "Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity," Trump wrote, before adding, "CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!" The president did not explain how eliminating the alleged corruption would balance the federal budget. Trump then pivoted to Iran, declaring that the United States no longer needs to negotiate a deal with Tehran. "We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote. "We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" Trump did not elaborate on his claims regarding Iranian funds or the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically important waterway for global energy shipments. articles.body:
Congress isn’t letting Nvidia’s Huang off the hook

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sent shockwaves across Silicon Valley and Washington, but the tensions seem far from over.

Lawmakers in Washington are still seeking answers and want to hear from Huang amid national security concerns his involvement with a woman who U.S. officials concluded was likely a spy.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.) said on Thursday the former Nvidia CEO “agreed to come” in for a briefing that will likely be “under oath, transcribed, video recorded,” though negotiations are ongoing on the details.

Huang admitted this week he had an affair with Alice Huang, a onetime executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed who is suspected of working as a Chinese intelligence asset.

The explosive revelations prompted bipartisan calls for an investigation into Huang and Nvidia, which don’t seem to be going away following his resignation.

House China Committee Chair John Moolenaar (Mich.) said it’s important that “we hear from him directly, as soon as possible.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) welcomed Huang’s resignation, but said it’s not enough to allay concerns about the potential threat.

“It was the right thing to do,” he said Thursday during a press conference in the Capitol. “Now we have to get to the bottom of whether America’s national security has been compromised.”

The incoming Speaker said Reps. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chairman of the Intelligence Committee, and Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), who’s expected to lead the Foreign Affairs panel, will take the lead for House Democrats as they dig into the national security implications of the Huang scandals.

“We’ve seen the tip of the iceberg,” Meeks told reporters. “The board probably did what it had to do. I have other questions. This doesn’t make it go away.”

articles.summary: Presented by CareQuest {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Top Dems: CMS must give states more time on Medicaid work rules Two top Democrats in the House and Senate are pushing the Trump administration to delay implementing Medicaid work reporting requirement on states, arguing there isn’t enough time for states to prepare before the Jan.…
articles.body:
Top Dems: CMS must give states more time on Medicaid work rules

Two top Democrats in the House and Senate are pushing the Trump administration to delay implementing Medicaid work reporting requirement on states, arguing there isn’t enough time for states to prepare before the Jan. 1 deadline.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.), who will likely lead the top committees with health jurisdiction next year, called on Trump administration officials to use their “discretion to give states additional time to implement work reporting requirements and protect eligible beneficiaries from losing coverage.”

The letter comes amid mounting uncertainty for states just weeks before the implementation deadline.

Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Medicaid expansion states must enact new Medicaid work reporting requirements beginning on Jan. 1, 2027.

The provision requires Medicaid enrollees between the ages of 19 and 65 to work, participate in community service, or attend an education program for at least 80 hours a month.

Republicans included a carve-out for people who are “medically frail,” and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services published a rule telling states how that term should be defined.

But the administration’s definition was much more restrictive than what states had prepared for, leading to some suing the administration.

Implementation of that provision was paused last month by a federal judge, who found that the administration’s definition of “medically frail” was unlawful.

But the administration plans to appeal the ruling, and the issue may not be resolved for months, creating enormous uncertainty for states about what the rules will be less than two months before the paperwork requirements take effect.

Failure “to permit states to delay implementation despite known operational deficiencies will worsen preventable coverage losses for which Congressional Democrats will hold the Trump Administration accountable,” the lawmakers wrote.

Pallone and Wyden noted that one of Democrats’ top priorities early next year will be repealing the nearly $1 trillion Medicaid cuts enacted under the OBBBA.

But until Congress acts, the lawmakers said CMS has a responsibility to carry out the law as Congress intended, “and to ensure that implementation does not unnecessarily jeopardize coverage for eligible beneficiaries.”

articles.title: Photos showing White House ballroom’s size spark backlash from Clyburn, McGarvey
articles.summary: Newly-released images showing the new White House ballroom’s size spark backlash among a pair of House Democrats — Reps. James Clyburn S.C(.) and Morgan McGarvey (Ky.) — who voiced their frustration with the project on social media this week. “I hope everyone takes a good hard look at this picture,” Clyburn wrote in a Wednesday…
articles.body:
Newly-released images showing the new White House ballroom’s size spark backlash among a pair of House Democrats — Reps. James Clyburn S.C(.) and Morgan McGarvey (Ky.) — who voiced their frustration with the project on social media this week.

“I hope everyone takes a good hard look at this picture,” Clyburn wrote in a Wednesday evening post to social platform X . “Trump’s under-construction ballroom is now bigger than the rest of the White House. Much bigger.”

“The contrast says everything you need to know about this President and his priorities,” the South Carolina lawmaker added.

The post also included a picture of the ballroom construction zone, in which the new structure looks noticeably taller than the executive residence. Photos of the White House a photographer with The Associated Press took Tuesday appeared similar to those Clyburn and McGarvey posted.

“This is what Trump is doing while millions of Americans can’t afford rent,” McGarvey wrote in a Thursday post using the same image.

The ballroom is one of several projects President Trump has undertaken in his effort to renovate the White House. It was the subject of litigation throughout this year as the president battled against conservation groups over the demolition of the East Wing to make way for the 90,000-square-foot ballroom on the White House campus.

His administration has argued the construction project was necessary for national security, while National Trust for Historic Preservation said the project exceeds Trump’s authority.

At a press conference shortly after the midterm election, Trump signed the final beam in the ballroom’s construction zone while standing with workers and other officials.

Trump called the ballroom “the most powerful building structurally … they say ever built and it was designed that way so the president can have safety.”

“It’s been the dream of presidents to have a ballroom for 150 years,” he continued.

The president originally said the addition would cost $400 million and be funded entirely by private donors. But a Washington Post report from late August suggested the cost could balloon to $600 million — with some of the funds allegedly needing to come from taxpayers’ pockets.
